rows.label: Concept
rows.text: A biopatent is a time-limited right over a genuine invention. Biopiracy is commercial use of a biological resource or of traditional knowledge without permission or benefit-sharing. Turmeric's wound-healing patent was revoked because the use was already known. Neem and basmati raised the same kind of objection, and recorded traditional knowledge is now used to stop repeat claims.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Biopiracy = resource or traditional knowledge + commercial use + no consent + no share of the benefit.
Prior art (old public knowledge) → novelty fails → patent revoked or refused.

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Holding a patent is not itself biopiracy. Biopiracy is taking knowledge or a resource without consent or payment.  ·  Turmeric's wound-healing patent was revoked. It is not an example of a patent India accepted.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Do not invent a patent number in the answer unless you are sure of it. The story and the outcome are what is marked.  ·  Name the community or the country as the party that was left out. Biopiracy is about people, not only about plants.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: The turmeric wound patent fell because Ayurvedic and other written use already existed.  ·  Neem extracts used as traditional fungicides were claimed in patents that opponents said lacked novelty.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Basmati was not invented in a US laboratory. It is a traditional variety. That is the point of the dispute.  ·  Documenting traditional knowledge is not the same as patenting it. The library is there so examiners can see that a claim is old.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Write a paragraph that defines both terms and then gives the turmeric case.  ·  Explain why writing traditional knowledge into a library protects it.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Patent = grant. Piracy = taking.  ·  Turmeric revoked. Basmati contested. Neem: traditional use, novelty attacked.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Why was the turmeric wound-healing patent revoked?  ·  How is a basmati patent dispute different from inventing a new drug molecule?

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Always separate the two terms before the examples. Examiners set the trap that they mean the same thing.  ·  Use turmeric as the revoked-patent example and basmati as the traditional-variety example. They are not the same case.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Biopatent versus biopiracy  ·  Novelty and prior traditional use  ·  Turmeric revocation  ·  Neem and basmati disputes

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Biopatent: a legal right over an invention.  ·  Biopiracy: commercial use without permission or benefit-sharing.  ·  Turmeric wound-healing patent: revoked after prior traditional use was shown.  ·  Neem patents were attacked because the uses were already traditional.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: A patent is refused or revoked when the claimed invention was already known.  ·  Biological resources are not ownerless just because they grow wild or were bred by farmers.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: What must a company do if it wants to use a community's medicinal plant fairly?

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: India objected to a US patent that tied the basmati name and its grain traits to a company's lines.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: Biopiracy means → B  ·  The US patent on turmeric for wound healing was → B

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: A biopatent is a legal right granted over an invention: a new process, a modified organism, or a product. It lasts for a set time and stops others from using that invention commercially without permission. The right is given by a patent office after a claim is examined.  ·  Biopiracy is the use of a community's biological resource or traditional knowledge for profit without permission, without naming the source, and without sharing the benefit. It is a taking. A patent is a grant. The two words are not synonyms.  ·  Turmeric has been used in India for wound healing for a very long time. A US patent was nonetheless issued on that use. India's Council of Scientific and Industrial Research showed the use was already documented traditional knowledge, and the patent was revoked.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Benefit-sharing and the knowledge library  ·  Basmati: RiceTec's patent was challenged by India.  ·  CSIR India led the turmeric challenge.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Benefit-sharing means money or other gains return to the source community, and use starts with permission.  ·  Novelty fails when the knowledge was already public in a traditional form.  ·  The country and the community that kept the resource are entitled to consent and a share.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: A searchable record of traditional knowledge is a defence against bad patents.  ·  Define biopatent and biopiracy in one sentence each.  ·  Tell the turmeric story in three steps: grant, challenge, result.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Say what the Traditional Knowledge Digital Library is for.  ·  Neem was the subject of patents on fungicidal and other uses that farmers already practised. Campaigns against those patents argued that the knowledge was not new. A patent requires novelty. Traditional use is evidence that the claim was not new.  ·  Basmati is a traditional aromatic rice of the Indian subcontinent. RiceTec obtained a US patent on rice lines and grains it marketed in connection with basmati. India challenged the patent because the name and the traits were tied to farmers' varieties, not to a new invention from outside that tradition.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Defences now include writing traditional knowledge down in a form patent examiners will search, such as India's Traditional Knowledge Digital Library, and requiring permission plus a share of profits before a foreign company uses a local resource. Benefit-sharing is the opposite of biopiracy.  ·  # Biopiracy and patent issues ## 1.
